traveler: Jalal al-Din Rumi (Mowlana Jalaluddin Muhammad Balkhi)
title: Balkh to Konya: the Sun of Tabriz and the Turning
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Balkh and the Flight Before the Mongols

stops.name: Balkh, the house of Baha al-Din Walad
stops.campa: In the merchant city of Balkh, gate of Khorasan, a son is born to Baha al-Din Walad, the preacher known through the province as Sultan al-Ulama, Sultan of the Scholars, whose sermons on the soul's encounter with God fill the great mosque past its doors. They name him Muhammad, called Jalal al-Din: Glory of the Faith. The house stands among gardens and canals under the shadow of the old citadel; scholars, dervishes and the sons of emirs pass daily through its rooms. No one yet says what the astrologers will later claim they saw written in his nativity.
suggested_refs: The house-mosque site of Baha al-Din Walad at Balkh, in present-day Balkh, Afghanistan
The old citadel (Bala Hissar) of Balkh, standing in Rumi's traditional birth-city
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Balkh, the Sultan of the Scholars and the philosophers' enmity
stops.campa: The boy grows in a house at war with the fashion of the age. Baha al-Din Walad thunders from the pulpit against the rationalist philosophers favored at the Khwarazmshah's court, calling their proofs a cage built around God; the court philosophers name him back a vulgar preacher and worse. Years of standing enmity gather over the family like weather. Baha al-Din begins to speak of departure, of a world about to be poured out like a cup, though what is truly gathering beyond the Oxus, in the felt tents of the Mongol camps, no one in Balkh has yet named.
suggested_refs: Baha al-Din Walad's Ma'arif (Divine Sciences), recording his sermons against the court philosophers
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Balkh, the dream that empties the city
stops.campa: In the year the world tips, Baha al-Din Walad gathers his household, his books, and the small son not yet twelve, and takes the western road. The tradition remembers a dream sent before the going out: the ground of Balkh opening like a sea, the whole standing world afloat and sinking. Within two years the actual sea will come: Genghis Khan's armies will break the city's walls, slaughter its people, and burn what the family left behind. Baha al-Din does not wait to see it. The caravan turns its face toward Nishapur, and behind it Balkh keeps counting down its years.
suggested_refs: The Mongol-sacked ruins of old Balkh (1220-21), the breach still visible at the Bala Hissar
genghis_khan.journey.json (the storm the family outran)

stops.name: Nishapur, blessed by Attar
stops.campa: In Nishapur, city of the perfumers and the poets, the caravan halts and the old sheikh Farid al-Din Attar receives them. He sees the father walking ahead of the small son and says the sentence the tradition will not let go: here comes a sea followed by an ocean. He calls the boy aside, puts into his hands his own book of the soul's entanglement in the world, the Asrarnama, the Book of Secrets, and tells those standing near that this child will soon set fire to the hearts of the world's lovers. Two years later the Mongols will take Attar's own life in this same city.
stops.quote: Here comes a sea followed by an ocean.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Farid al-Din Attar on receiving the family at Nishapur (Dowlatshah, Tadhkirat al-Shu'ara; Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin)
suggested_refs: Attar's Asrarnama, the Book of Secrets, said to have been given to the boy Rumi
attar.journey.json (Attar's own death in the Mongol sack of Nishapur, 1221, shared pin)
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Baghdad, thirty days at the tomb of Junayd
stops.campa: The road west brings the family to Baghdad, seat of the Caliphate, city of a thousand years of the science of hearts. Baha al-Din will not lodge in the khanqahs of the great sheikhs, saying he has no need of any teacher but the one within; but he permits the household a month's rest, and the boy is taken to pray at the tombs of the old masters of the Sufi path, Junayd and Ma'ruf al-Karkhi among them, whose sayings on annihilation in God he will echo, unknowing, in verses not yet written. The caravan turns south, toward the House of God.
suggested_refs: The shrine-tomb of Junayd of Baghdad, foundational teacher of the sober school of Sufism

segments.name: The Pilgrim Road: Mecca to the Anatolian Marches

stops.name: Mecca, the circling of the Kaaba
stops.campa: Baha al-Din Walad leads his household through the desert to perform the Hajj, the duty owed once in a life. The boy who will one day write that the lovers of God have a Kaaba of their own, built of the heart and needing no stone, circles here the actual House, the black corner-stone, the well of Zamzam, among the thousands of the pilgrimage year. Whatever is later made of it in verse, the canon insists the actual dust of Mecca is under his feet this once: the outward rite performed in full before the inward one is ever spoken of.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Masjid al-Haram, Mecca, station of the family's Hajj
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Damascus, the child before Ibn al-Arabi
stops.campa: Returning north from the pilgrimage the family rests in Damascus, city of jasmine and the Umayyad minarets. The tradition preserves one meeting here that later ages will marvel at: the great Shaykh al-Akbar, Muhyi al-Din Ibn al-Arabi, watches Baha al-Din Walad cross a courtyard with his son a pace behind, and says to those beside him, in wonder, praise be to God, an ocean walking behind a lake. Neither master nor boy yet knows what the boy will become; the sentence is set down anyway, waiting, like the Asrarnama, for its own fulfillment.
stops.quote: Praise be to God! An ocean walking behind a lake!
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Ibn al-Arabi on seeing the boy Rumi behind his father in Damascus (later Mevlevi hagiographic tradition)
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Mosque of Damascus, where Ibn al-Arabi taught and prayed
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West (on the tradition's historicity)

stops.name: Malatya, the bread of exile
stops.campa: Word comes that the Mongols have taken Samarkand and are pouring into Khorasan; the family does not turn back. They cross into Anatolian lands under Seljuk rule, safe for now behind the Taurus passes, and settle for a time in Malatya, an Armenian and Turkish town of weavers and copper-smiths on the old caravan road. Baha al-Din teaches; the boy studies grammar, law, and the Qur'an at his father's knee and among his father's students. Refugees from the eastern provinces keep arriving with worse news each season: Balkh fallen, Nishapur fallen, Attar himself among the dead of that second city.
suggested_refs: The medieval citadel of Malatya (Eski Malatya / Battalgazi), station of the family's Anatolian exile
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Erzincan, the patronage of the Malika Ismati Khatun
stops.campa: From Malatya the family moves to Erzincan, called to the court of the Malika Ismati Khatun, wife of the Mengujekid ruler, who has heard of the wandering scholar's fame and builds him a madrasa in her city. For a season the family knows a settled roof and a princely patron; Baha al-Din completes pages of his Ma'arif here, dictating the visions and spiritual states that will one day astonish his son when he finds the manuscript again in Konya and reads his dead father's inner life for the first time, weeping over sentences he had never been told.
suggested_refs: Baha al-Din Walad's Ma'arif, later read by Rumi himself as his father's spiritual diary
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Larende (Karaman), seven years, the marriage to Gowhar Khatun
stops.campa: The family settles longest at Larende, the town later ages will call Karaman, where Baha al-Din is given a post at last with some permanence. Here the wandering pauses seven years, long enough for the boy to become a young man formed equally in law and in longing. On his father's arrangement he marries Gowhar Khatun, daughter of a fellow exile from Samarkand, Sharaf al-Din Lala; the wedding is kept in the plain style of scholars, without the ceremony a court would have given a Sultan of the Learned's son. The road that carried him from Balkh finally sets down, for a while, a household.
suggested_refs: The old quarter of Karaman (Larende), where the family kept seven settled years
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Larende, the birth of Sultan Walad
stops.campa: A son is born to Jalal al-Din and Gowhar Khatun and named Baha al-Din Muhammad after his grandfather, though the world will remember him by his title, Sultan Walad: he will grow to be his father's first biographer, the keeper of the Shams story in his own Persian verse, and, when the turning founds itself into an order after his father's death, its true architect. A second son, Ala al-Din Muhammad, will follow within a few years. In this small provincial house at Larende, without any of the parties knowing it, the whole future government of the Mevlevi order is already asleep in its cradle.
suggested_refs: Sultan Walad's own Ibtidanama (Valadnama), the primary verse-chronicle of his father's life
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

segments.name: Konya: The Sultan's Seat, the Father's Grave, the Hidden Teacher

stops.name: Konya, arrival at the sultan's invitation
stops.campa: The Seljuk sultan of Rum, Ala al-Din Kayqubad, builder-king of a capital he means to make the ornament of Anatolia, invites the renowned Sultan of the Learned to his city and grants the family a madrasa of their own. Konya receives them: a walled city of blue-tiled minarets under the shadow of Alaeddin Hill, crossed by trade roads from Iran, Syria and the Byzantine coast, thick with jurists, poets and dervishes of every stripe. Baha al-Din takes up his last post here. Jalal al-Din, twenty-two years old, does not yet know that every remaining stone of his life will be laid in this one city.
suggested_refs: The Alaeddin Mosque and citadel hill of Konya, seat of Kayqubad's Seljuk capital

stops.name: Konya, the death of the Sultan of the Learned
stops.campa: Baha al-Din Walad dies in Konya in his seventies, having taught to the last, and the whole city is said to close its shops for his funeral: the sultan himself among the mourners, so great a crowd that the bier can barely pass through the streets to the rose garden set aside for the sultan's own family, where he is laid to rest. Jalal al-Din, twenty-three, inherits his father's students, his father's pulpit, and, though he does not fully know it yet, his father's unfinished path into the hidden sciences of the heart, which the young man has so far touched only through law and grammar.
suggested_refs: The Sultan's Rose Garden mausoleum at Konya, Baha al-Din Walad's grave, later beneath the Green Dome

stops.name: Konya, Rumi mounts the pulpit
stops.campa: The students of the dead master turn to the son, and Jalal al-Din takes up his father's chair: a young jurist and preacher already learned enough, by every outward measure, to be counted among the great teachers of the age, expounding Hanafi law and Qur'anic commentary to hundreds. He is respected, sought after, correct in every visible particular of the scholar's life. What his father's manuscripts, and his father's God, asked of a man beyond correctness he has not yet been shown; that showing is still thirteen years and one strange old wanderer away.
suggested_refs: The Konya madrasa where Rumi inherited his father's chair, near the site of the later Mevlana complex
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, Sayyid Burhan al-Din tests the son against the father
stops.campa: A dust-worn dervish arrives at Konya's gate: Sayyid Burhan al-Din Muhaqqiq of Termez, a former student of Baha al-Din's own youth, come from the east too late to see his teacher living. He goes first to weep at the grave, then seeks out the son, and delivers a verdict that unmans the young professor's confidence: in outward learning you have surpassed your father, but in the inward path, the science of states and stations that made him what he was, you are still lacking. Jalal al-Din, stung and humbled, submits himself as a disciple to his father's former student. Nine years of hidden schooling begin.
stops.quote: In learning you have surpassed your father, but in the inward path you are still lacking.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sayyid Burhan al-Din Muhaqqiq (Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin; Mevlevi oral tradition)
suggested_refs: The tomb of Sayyid Burhan al-Din Muhaqqiq at Kayseri, where he later taught and died
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Aleppo and Damascus, the years of the Halawiyya and the circle of the shaykhs
stops.campa: On Burhan al-Din's order the young scholar goes south again, this time as a man, to complete his formal learning: years at the Halawiyya madrasa of Aleppo, seat of Hanafi jurisprudence, and after it in Damascus, where the greatest Sufis of the age are gathered. Tradition holds that he now sits among the discourses he only glimpsed as a child: the aging Shaykh al-Akbar Ibn al-Arabi, his brilliant stepson-disciple Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, who will one day be his neighbor and friend in Konya, and the controversial contemplative Awhad al-Din Kirmani. He returns west a finished jurist who has breathed the same rooms as the theorists of the Oneness of Being.
suggested_refs: The Halawiyya Madrasa of Aleppo, seat of Rumi's advanced jurisprudence
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West
William Chittick, The Sufi Path of Love

stops.name: Konya, the return, the forty-day seclusions, and the death of Burhan al-Din
stops.campa: Back in Konya, Burhan al-Din sets his pupil to a discipline no madrasa taught: chilla after chilla, forty-day seclusions of fasting and prayer in a locked cell, until the sayyid pronounces him complete, without equal in the world, he says, in the outward sciences as in the hidden ones, and releases him to teach on his own authority. Not long after, the old master dies at Kayseri. Jalal al-Din is now, in the eyes of Konya, everything a Sultan of the Learned's son should be: mufti to hundreds of students, jurist consulted by the city's judges, a man entirely respectable. He has no idea what is coming to unmake him.
stops.quote: Without equal in the world, in the outward sciences as in the hidden ones.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sayyid Burhan al-Din Muhaqqiq on completing Rumi's training (Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin)
suggested_refs: The tomb of Sayyid Burhan al-Din Muhaqqiq at Kayseri

stops.name: Konya, the Inn of the Sugar Merchants, a stranger seizes the bridle
stops.campa: A wandering dervish in black felt, called Shams al-Din of Tabriz, the Flier, for he has never stayed anywhere long, comes to lodge at the Inn of the Sugar Merchants in Konya. As the renowned professor rides through the square surrounded by students, the stranger steps out and seizes his bridle: which is greater, he demands, the Prophet Muhammad, who said, we have not known You, God, as You should be known, or Bayazid Bistami, who said, glory be to me, how great is my station? Rumi, furious at the impertinence, answers that Muhammad's unknowing surpasses all Bayazid's claiming, and falls from his mount in a faint at the force of his own answer.
stops.quote: The Prophet's 'we have not known You as You should be known' surpasses Bayazid's 'glory be to me' — for Bayazid's thirst was small enough to be satisfied by a single drop, and he cried that he was full, while the Prophet's vessel could never be filled, and he thirsted on.
stops.quote_source: The traditional form of Rumi's answer to Shams of Tabriz, transmitted in Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin, and Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama
suggested_refs: The Şekerciler (Sugar Merchants') Han site in Konya's old bazaar, traditional site of the meeting
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, the forty days behind the locked door
stops.campa: Rumi takes the stranger home. For forty days, by the account the order keeps, the two men shut themselves into a cell and see no one; food is passed through the door, and no word of what passes between them is ever fully told, only that a Sultan of the Learned's son emerges a different man, one to whom the outward sciences that made his name are now, he says, like carrion beside the feast Shams has set before him. Konya's foremost professor stops lecturing on law. His students, who had queued for his rulings, now find him instead composing verses and turning, unannounced, in the middle of the room.
suggested_refs: The Diwan-e Shams-e Tabrizi, the great outpouring that begins in this seclusion

stops.name: Konya, the disciples murmur, Shams reads the danger
stops.campa: The professor's abandonment of the pulpit for a penniless wanderer scandalizes Konya's learned circle. Students who once vied for his classes now find their teacher lost to them, closeted for days with a man of no lineage and no known school, who speaks to their master as an equal and sometimes as a master himself. Whispers turn to threats; some of the household, even, the tradition says, resent the stranger's hold on Rumi's heart. Shams, who has fled more cities than he has settled in, reads the coming danger in the mutterings at the door and, one winter night, without warning, is simply gone.
suggested_refs: The Diwan-e Shams, ghazals of separation composed in the months of Shams's first absence
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Damascus, the first flight of the sun
stops.campa: Shams surfaces in Damascus, the city Rumi himself once studied in, and there he stays while, in Konya, the teacher he left behind falls into a grief the canon records almost as illness: weeks of silence, verses composed and destroyed, students turned away. Letters go out searching every direction. Word finally comes of the wanderer's whereabouts, and it is not Rumi himself but his own son, Sultan Walad, not yet twenty, who sets out on the road to Damascus to beg the sun of Tabriz to return and warm Konya again.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad quarter of Damascus, Shams's refuge in his first flight
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, Sultan Walad rides to bring him home
stops.campa: Sultan Walad finds Shams in Damascus and delivers his father's letters, written in verse, pleading and abject with love. Shams relents and returns with the young man, who, the son's own chronicle records with plain pride, walks the last miles on foot beside Shams's mount out of reverence, though offered a horse himself. Rumi and Shams are reunited in a scene the whole city gathers to watch, weeping, neither man able to say afterward which of them fell at the other's feet first. For a season the two are inseparable again, and the teaching of the pulpit is not resumed.
stops.quote: They fell at each other's feet, and no one knew who was the lover and who the beloved.
stops.quote_source: Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama, on the reunion of Rumi and Shams (April 1247)
suggested_refs: Sultan Walad's Ibtidanama, sole eyewitness account of the reunion journey

stops.name: Konya, the marriage of Shams and Kimya Khatun
stops.campa: To settle Shams among them and quiet the household's unease, Rumi arranges his marriage to Kimya Khatun, a girl raised since childhood in his own house, daughter of his second wife Kira Khatun by an earlier marriage. It is meant as an anchor, a reason for the wandering dervish to keep an address in Konya at last. But the marriage does not calm the jealousy circling Shams; within the household some still resent him bitterly for what he has taken from their teacher, and the bride herself, not yet strong, begins to fail under the strain of a house at war with itself around her.
suggested_refs: The women's quarters of Rumi's household in medieval Konya, Kimya Khatun's upbringing
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, the last night, the cry in the dark
stops.campa: On a night in early winter, the account preserved by the order says, Shams and Rumi are sitting together when someone comes to the door and calls Shams out. He rises, saying to Rumi, I am called to be killed, and goes into the dark and is never seen alive again. Seven men, some say including Rumi's own second son Ala al-Din, are afterward named by rumor in his death; a body is said to have been found long after in a well near the house, and quietly laid, some accounts say, beside Baha al-Din Walad's own grave. The sun of Tabriz has set, this time for good.
stops.quote: I am called to be killed.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Shams of Tabriz on the night of his disappearance (Mevlevi oral tradition, later Ottoman-era chroniclers)
suggested_refs: The Makam-i Shems (Shrine of Shams) in Konya, traditional resting place venerated near the Green Dome
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West
Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama (silence on the fate, later filled by tradition)

stops.name: Damascus, the search, and the turning inward
stops.campa: Not believing, or not able to bear believing, that Shams will not return, Rumi rides to Damascus himself, twice, searching every quarter and every khanqah for the face he has not stopped seeing. It is here, the tradition holds, walking a city he already knows from his student years, that the search turns over inside him like a key in a lock: why should I seek? I am the same as he; his own essence speaks through me; I have been looking for myself. He rides back to Konya not with Shams beside him, but as a man who has stopped needing him to be.
stops.quote: Why should I seek? I am the same as He. His essence speaks through me. I have been looking for myself.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Rumi's realization in Damascus, within the transmitted teaching of the Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi
suggested_refs: The Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi, forty thousand verses written in Shams's name after his disappearance
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, the marketplace of the goldbeaters, the first turning
stops.campa: Passing through the market of the goldsmiths, Rumi hears, from the shop of Salah al-Din the goldbeater, the rhythmic chime of hammers thinning gold leaf, tak, tak, tak, striking a beat that seems to his ear to say the first words of the confession of faith, there is no god but God. Something in him that has been grieving since Shams's silence answers the sound with his body before his mind can stop it: he lifts his arms and turns where he stands, again and again, in the open street, while astonished shoppers and apprentices gather to watch a Sultan of the Learned's son spin like a dervish among the anvils.
suggested_refs: The traditional site of the goldsmiths' bazaar in old Konya, birthplace of the sema
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, Salah al-Din Zarkub, the second sun
stops.campa: Rumi does not merely spare the goldsmith's embarrassment; he takes Salah al-Din Zarkub as his companion in Shams's place, an unlettered, humble man who cannot always speak correctly and is mocked for it by the jealous, yet whom Rumi elevates above every learned disciple, saying the man's very errors of grammar are dearer to him than the eloquence of scholars. For ten years Salah al-Din anchors him: no ecstatic flight this time but a steady, undemonstrative love, proof that the sun which burned in Shams can also warm quietly, in a shop that smells of solder and gold-dust, in a friend who asks nothing.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Salah al-Din Zarkub, near the Mevlana complex in Konya
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, the wedding of Sultan Walad and Fatima Khatun
stops.campa: Rumi binds the two houses of his heart together: his own son Sultan Walad, who once rode to Damascus for Shams's sake, marries Fatima Khatun, Salah al-Din the goldsmith's daughter. It is the marriage that will run the whole future of the order through Salah al-Din's blood as much as Rumi's own, for it is Sultan Walad and Fatima's descendants who will govern the Mevlevi lineage for centuries after. Rumi presides over the wedding himself, and the household that survived Shams's death and the city's suspicion finds, in this quieter union, something like the peace the earlier love never had room for.
suggested_refs: The genealogical line of Chelebi leadership descending from Sultan Walad and Fatima Khatun
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, the death of the unlettered saint
stops.campa: Salah al-Din Zarkub dies in Konya after ten years at Rumi's side, and the funeral, the order remembers, is kept not with mourning but with music and the sema, drums and reed-flutes playing in the funeral procession itself, for Rumi will not permit death to be met with anything but the same turning that meets God. He composes verses for the goldsmith's passing that read less like elegy than wedding-song: a soul let out at last into its true country. Konya has now lost, within eleven years, both suns that taught its most famous scholar how to burn.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Salah al-Din Zarkub, still visited near the Mevlana museum complex

stops.name: Konya, Husam al-Din Chelebi, third and last companion
stops.campa: Even before Salah al-Din's death, a younger disciple has begun to take a place at Rumi's side that will outlast them all: Husam al-Din Chelebi, son of the head of a guild of akhis, the Anatolian brotherhoods of chivalry and craft, a man of some wealth who gives it all to the order and asks in return only nearness. Where Shams was the fire and Salah al-Din the steady coal, Husam al-Din becomes the hand that will finally catch what burns in Rumi and set it down in ink: without him, the order will always say, the great poem would never have been written at all.
suggested_refs: The dedication verses of the Masnavi naming Husam al-Din its cause and scribe
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: The vineyards of Meram, the verses drawn from the turban
stops.campa: Walking with Rumi among the vineyards of Meram outside the city, Husam al-Din makes his request: the disciples read Sanai's Hadiqa and Attar's Mantiq al-Tayr for guidance on the path; would the master not compose a book of his own in that same rhymed-couplet form, that they might drink from a nearer well? Rumi, without a pause, reaches into the folds of his turban and draws out a paper already written, the first eighteen verses of the reed's own complaint, as if the poem had been waiting inside his clothing for the question to be asked. Dictation begins that hour and does not stop for years.
stops.quote: Listen to the reed, how it tells a tale, complaining of separations: 'Ever since I was parted from the reed-bed, my lament hath caused man and woman to moan.'
stops.quote_source: Masnavi, Book I, opening verses (trans. R. A. Nicholson)
suggested_refs: The reed-flute (ney), instrument of the Masnavi's opening image and of the sema ceremony
The Konya autograph Masnavi manuscript (Mevlana Museum, MS 51)

stops.name: Konya, the two years of silence
stops.campa: The dictation of the first book, taken down as Rumi walks, teaches, bathes, even in the middle of the night when Husam al-Din must be roused to write, breaks off after some four thousand couplets and falls silent for nearly two years: Husam al-Din's own wife has died, and grief closes the channel between them. When it reopens, the second book begins with an apology in verse for the long delay, the poem itself noting its own interruption, a rare moment where the Masnavi turns and looks at the circumstances of its own making before returning to its river of stories.
stops.quote: The composition of the Masnavi has been delayed for a season: an interval was needed in order that the blood might turn to milk.
stops.quote_source: Masnavi, Book II, opening verses on the delay (trans. R. A. Nicholson)
suggested_refs: The six-book structure of the Masnavi, its internal seam still visible at this interruption
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, the sessions at the pulpit, Fihi ma Fihi
stops.campa: Alongside the great poem, students in these years set down, unbidden by Rumi himself, the informal talks he gives at gatherings and in answer to visiting notables: seventy-one sessions of plain, often startling prose that will be gathered after his death as Fihi ma Fihi, In It What Is In It. Here he speaks without the reed-flute's veil, telling a Mongol governor that outward conquest is nothing beside the conquest of one's own anger, telling a grieving mother that a child's death is a door and not a wall. The talk is looser than the poem, and in some ways franker.
stops.quote: The Qur'an is like a bride. Although you pull the veil away from her face, she does not show herself to you... but if you attract her by gentleness, she will show her face to you, unveiled, without any request or effort on your part.
stops.quote_source: Fihi ma Fihi (Discourses), in the translation of William C. Chittick
suggested_refs: Fihi ma Fihi, the prose discourses transcribed by disciples in Rumi's own idiom
sources: Rumi, Fihi ma Fihi, trans. Arberry
Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, six books, twenty-six thousand verses
stops.campa: By the last year of his life the Masnavi runs to six books and something over twenty-five thousand couplets, a poem the order will come to call the Qur'an in Persian, though Rumi himself calls it only the shop of unity, where nothing is sold but the One. Book Six ends without the formal close the earlier books were given, its final story of three princes broken off mid-argument, as if the reed had simply been lifted from the poet's lips before the last note. Husam al-Din will outlive him barely a decade; the unfinished ending is left exactly as the dictation left it.
suggested_refs: The complete six-book Masnavi, unfinished at Book Six's close
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, the final illness
stops.campa: In his sixty-sixth year Rumi's strength fails through an early winter of earthquakes and bad omens that the city reads, in hindsight, as portents. Physicians are sent by the Seljuk court and by the Mongol governor Mu'in al-Din Pervane, who has long counted himself among the poet's admirers; none can arrest the fever. Rumi asks for a basin of water and bathes his feet, his chest, his forehead in it from time to time, and between these small acts recites poetry to those gathered, most of it, those present remember, about the joy and not the sorrow of what is coming.
stops.quote: Do as you are commanded; you will find me, God willing, among those who are patiently submitting.
stops.quote_source: Qur'an 37:102, recited by Rumi in his last illness, recorded in Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin
suggested_refs: Historical earthquakes recorded in Konya, autumn-winter 1273, read by the city as omens of the death to come
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, 'Am I a thief?' — the death
stops.campa: On the fifth of Jumada al-Thani, the seventeenth of December by the Latin count, as the sun goes down, Rumi dies in his house in Konya. His wife Kira Khatun, weeping, begs him not to leave her; he answers her, the canon says, almost lightly, with a question that becomes his last recorded words: am I a thief, that you would hold me back, confine me here, and keep me from being joined again to my Love? The order will call this night, ever after, Sheb-i Arus, the Wedding Night: not a death observed but a marriage consummated, the reed returned at last to the reed-bed.
stops.quote: Am I a thief? Have I stolen someone's goods? Is this why you would confine me here and keep me from being rejoined with my Love?
stops.quote_source: Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin, on Rumi's death, 17 December 1273
suggested_refs: Sheb-i Arus, the annual 'Wedding Night' commemoration still kept at Konya every 17 December
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, the funeral of every faith
stops.campa: Word of the death runs through Konya faster than the criers can carry it, and the funeral the next day draws, the tradition insists, not only Muslims but the city's Christians and Jews into the same weeping crowd, each reading aloud from their own scripture as the bier passes. Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, Ibn al-Arabi's own stepson and Rumi's neighbor of many years, is given the honor of leading the funeral prayer, but is so overcome, some say by a vision of the Prophet and his angels walking the procession, that he faints before it is finished, and Husam al-Din Chelebi completes the prayer in his place.
suggested_refs: The funeral procession of Rumi as illustrated in later Ottoman manuscripts (e.g. the Morgan Library's Rumi cycle)
sources: The Morgan Library & Museum, 'The Funeral of Jalal Al-Din Rumi'

stops.name: Konya, burial beneath the Green Dome
stops.campa: Rumi is laid in the ground beside his father in the Sultan's rose garden, and over the grave the city, and later the Seljuk and Karamanid and Ottoman patrons who follow, raise the tower of glazed turquoise tile the whole world will come to know as the Green Dome, the Kubbe-i Hadra. Ala al-Din Kayqubad's madrasa around it becomes, in time, a lodge, then a museum, then again, quietly, a place of pilgrimage regardless of what any government has called it. The dome still stands over both graves, father and son, sea and the ocean that outgrew it, in the same small plot of Konya earth.
suggested_refs: The Green Dome (Kubbe-i Hadra / Yeşil Türbe) of the Mevlana Museum complex, Konya, Rumi's tomb
sources: UNESCO and Turkish Ministry of Culture records, Mevlana Museum

stops.name: Konya, Husam al-Din Chelebi, the first regent of the order
stops.campa: By Rumi's own wish, spoken before his death, Husam al-Din Chelebi, the scribe of the Masnavi, takes his place at the head of the disciples: the first postnishin, the one who sits on the sheepskin, of what has not yet a name of its own but will become the Mevlevi order. For ten years he holds the circle together, dictating nothing new, only guarding what has been dictated, until his own death passes the seat briefly to another elder disciple, Karim al-Din Baktamur, before it comes, as the blood and the poetry both intended all along, to Rumi's own son.
suggested_refs: The line of Chelebi succession beginning with Husam al-Din Chelebi as first postnishin
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, Sultan Walad braids the order and the rite of the turning
stops.campa: Sultan Walad, the boy once sent to Damascus to fetch Shams home, becomes at last the full head of the brotherhood his father never formally founded, and does what his father, lost always in the poem and the turning, never had time to do: gives the sema a fixed order of movements, the black cloak shed for the white, the tall camel-hair hat raised like a tombstone, the arms crossed and then opened to sky and earth; writes his own Ibtidanama and Rabab-nama to keep the story straight for pupils who never saw Shams; and sends the first Mevlevi lodges outward from Konya along the roads his grandfather once fled down in the other direction.
suggested_refs: Sultan Walad's codified Sema ceremony, still performed by the Mevlevi order today
Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama and Rabab-nama, the order's founding texts
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: From Konya to Sarajevo and Galata, the order's far branches
stops.campa: The turning outlives every empire that hosts it: Seljuk, Karamanid, six centuries of Ottoman patronage, lodges rising from Cairo to Aleppo to Sarajevo to the domed hall at Galata above the Bosphorus, each teaching the same forty-day cell, the same reed-cry, the same wheel of the arms. In 1925 the new Republic closes every tekke by law, Konya's own included; the dervishes turn in secret, or not at all, for decades, until UNESCO names the sema a Masterpiece of Humanity's Heritage in 2005, and the wheel turns openly again, at the Hadži Sinan tekke where a Sarajevo boy once watched it, at the Galata house where a seeker once had its mathematics explained to him.
suggested_refs: The 2005 UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage listing for the Mevlevi Sema ceremony
